bib.title: SPoC: Search-based Pseudocode to Code
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2019 (PDF is the arXiv v1 'Preprint. Under review')

question: Can long, functionally correct programs be synthesized from line-by-line pseudocode plus test cases by searching over translations, and can compiler-error credit assignment make that search cheaper?
hypothesis: Localizing which pseudocode line's translation caused a compile error and focusing search there beats uninformed best-first search under a fixed compilation budget.
contributions: SPoC dataset: 18,356 C++ programs with human-authored line-level pseudocode and ~38.6 test cases each
Evaluation by functional correctness (hidden test cases) at a budget of B synthesis trials
Two error-localization methods: multiclass classifier and prefix-based pruning

method.summary: A seq2seq model proposes 100 candidate code lines per pseudocode line; best-first search over line combinations compiles and tests programs on public tests until one passes or the budget runs out. Error localization (neural multiclass line predictor, or prefix-based pruning via extra compiles) down-weights or blacklists offending candidates.

datasets.name: SPoC
datasets.size: 18,356 programs, 677 problems, 59 annotators; avg 14.7 lines, 38.6 tests
datasets.split: TESTP: 158 held-out problems (1,820 programs, 10.1%); TESTW: 7 held-out workers (1,752 programs, 9.7%, 186 overlap with TESTP); rest train/dev 90:10
datasets.source: Codeforces accepted C++ solutions to easiest-level problems; pseudocode from Amazon Mechanical Turk workers
datasets.preprocessing: Filtered programs with #define, classes, structs, templates, switch, malloc; single-statement blocks grouped with preceding control statement

models.name: seq2seq line translator
models.architecture: LSTM encoder-decoder with attention-based copying and coverage vector (OpenNMT)

models.name: multiclass error localizer
models.architecture: three LSTMs (pseudocode line, code line, error message) + positional encoding of line offset, feedforward line embedding, LSTM across lines, feedforward logits, softmax

training.objective: log-likelihood (translation: p(code line | pseudocode line); localizer: log-likelihood of offending line on programs with one gold line replaced by a generated candidate that fails to compile)

inference.decoding: beam search per line (M=100) then best-first search over combinations by product of line probabilities, heap-based
inference.samples: deterministic search; budget B = synthesis trials (one compile + run on public tests); budgets in Fig 4 table: 10, 100, 1000, 3000

parameters.budget_unit: each additional compiler call in prefix pruning counts as one trial

metrics.name: success rate at B
metrics.definition: fraction of test examples where the system outputs a program that compiles and passes all public and hidden tests within B trials; the final program is checked on hidden tests, search sees only public tests

metrics.name: line-level functional correctness
metrics.definition: replace gold line y_i by candidate c_ij and check the program still passes public and hidden tests

metrics.name: trials reduction
metrics.definition: change in number of trials vs plain best-first search (absolute and relative; mean, median, geometric mean)

eval.protocol: single run per configuration (no seeds or intervals stated); two test sets TESTP and TESTW

limits: Only compile errors (88.7% of failures) are used for credit assignment; runtime and wrong-answer failures give only the sparse pass/fail signal.
Oracle ceiling (55.2%/71.4%) assumes incorrect candidates never combine into correct behaviour.
Programs are from easiest Codeforces problems; C++ only; line-aligned pseudocode is required.
Multiclass localizer is unverified and can catastrophically break an otherwise solvable case (1.6% succeeded->fails).
Training hyperparameters, alpha, optimizer, hardware and seeds are not given; single runs with no variance.
Abstract (25.6%) and introduction (24.6%) disagree on the top-one success rate; the 44.7% headline is not directly readable from Fig 4 cells.

Public tests drive search and hidden tests only judge the final program, so the success rate counts hidden-test generalisation, but the paper does not report how often a public-pass program fails hidden tests.
